result:
The sentence needs changes before publishing — both claims are risky as written.

**"Fully compliant with the framework"** — NIST SP 800-61 is a guideline, not a certifiable standard with a checklist you pass/fail. Claiming "full compliance" implies you've mapped every recommendation in the document to your workflow and verified it, which is a strong, checkable claim. Unless someone has actually done that gap analysis, this overclaims. Safer alternatives:
- "Our workflow is informed by/aligned with NIST SP 800-61" (if you drew on it but didn't do a formal mapping)
- "Our workflow follows the incident-response lifecycle described in NIST SP 800-61" (if you specifically mirror its phases — preparation, detection/analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, post-incident)

Only keep "fully compliant" if you can point to the actual mapping/audit that supports it.

**The SRE talk with no citation** — citing "a great talk we saw at a conference" with no name, speaker, or link isn't a real citation; it's an unverifiable claim dressed up as one. Two honest paths:
1. Track down the actual talk (search your calendar/conference program) and cite it properly, or
2. Drop the specific attribution and just describe the influence generically: "we also drew on common SRE incident-response practices" — no false specificity, nothing a reader can't check because there's nothing to check.

Publishing it as-is with an admitted missing citation is the main red flag — it signals to readers there's a real source you're just not bothering to produce, which reads as sloppy or evasive rather than honest.
